name: Daria Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government. We do not sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the late chat shift at a contact centre, so I watch the queue while answering the cases that keep reopening. I have a two-year college diploma and I use AI most days to search past replies, but I read the actual account before sending anything. I like catching an error before a customer has to call twice; the shift pattern makes it hard to see friends on weekdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the chat team the small tools are handy for spelling and finding order numbers, and I'd still want a human to own the answer. Customers can tell when someone just pastes a tidy sentence without reading the complaint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day, so I don't feel threatened by a little more of it. But I'm paid near the bottom of the lead range, and the money I have saved wouldn't cover a month without shifts; the ordinary bills are the real pressure here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the late chats and checking the refund queue, then set up an automatic transfer on payday. In the first year of this plateau, I'd use the same tools to catch duplicate complaints and put the time saved into coaching new agents, as long as my shifts stay full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a working week I know how to handle. I'm still not relaxed about my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do that the spelling tool cannot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I saw three complaints from one customer last week that looked like three separate cases. I joined them before she was charged twice, and then I called her; the neat draft would not have noticed the account history.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much can you move on payday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't promise a big amount until I see each month's bills. I'd start with a small fixed transfer, and I'd raise it after two months if I have not had to pull the money back.

S0.quote: Customers can tell when someone just pastes a tidy sentence without reading the complaint.
say: I would praise AI for **spelling** and searching while insisting a person owns each answer.
I would remind colleagues that customers notice a **pasted reply** that misses their complaint.
think: I use AI daily, but **low pay** and less than one month saved still worry me.
My **account history** skills matter even when routine messages get quicker.
do: Keep handling **late chats** and checking the refund queue.
Set a small **payday transfer** and review the amount after two months.
Use saved chat time to **coach new agents** if shifts stay full.
feel: **Steady** at work, unsettled by the account balance.
fieldNote: Daria describes AI as an everyday **work tool**, yet she does not confuse convenience with household security.
Her example of linked complaints shows a specific **judgment skill** beyond tidy writing.

steps.text: Keep handling late customer chats and checking refund cases
Transfer a small fixed amount on each payday
Use AI to find duplicate complaints before coaching new agents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should be the people who test the new system, because we know where a polished reply can still be wrong. I'd put screenshots of failures in the team channel and ask for paid time to check them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our centre answers chats and calls, exactly the kind of thinking work that changes first. I could become useful in testing the system, but that might be one testing job where there are now several agents, and I can't count on winning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd build a small folder of wrong AI replies, with customer details removed, and ask my manager to let me run a trial. In the first year after rollout, I'd apply for the quality testing shift if it opens; if my regular hours drop, I'd offer evening spreadsheet help to local shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel switched on and worried at the same time. I like making tools work, but I know a clever tool can leave somebody without rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should count corrected refunds and repeat calls, not just faster typing. I'd ask my colleague Jo to mark the same cases by hand, so we could see what the tool misses before anyone raises targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra work leave you time for evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not every evening. I'd try one shop first, on a night I'm not on late chats, and stop if it meant I was too tired to check customer records carefully.

S1.quote: I like making tools work, but I know a clever tool can leave somebody without rent.
say: I would ask agents to **test failures** before the centre makes AI replies standard.
I would ask for **paid checking time** instead of higher targets based only on speed.
think: I see one possible **testing role** replacing several chat shifts.
I might win that role, but my **thin savings** make the gamble serious.
do: Collect **wrong replies** without customer details and ask for a trial.
Apply for a **quality testing** shift if one opens after rollout.
Offer one nearby shop **spreadsheet help** if regular hours fall.
feel: **Energised** by testing and anxious about lost wages.
fieldNote: Daria wants to measure **repeat calls** and refund corrections, not typing speed alone.
Her proposed side work is deliberately **small** because tiredness could hurt her main job.

steps.text: Collect anonymised AI reply errors and request a trial
Apply for a quality testing shift after rollout if one opens
Offer one local shop evening spreadsheet help if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that our testing notes belong in any plan for change, and that people need paid routes into other work. I wouldn't sell the idea that everyone can become a tool supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AGI can handle almost every thinking task by 2028, even my proposed quality role could vanish. Robots aren't due until around 2031, but they are not the reason my phone and chat work is at risk. I have less than a month saved and very little time to build more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book a meeting with the staff group now and ask for written notice and training pay. I'd also contact the college about a short health aide course, but in the first year after AGI arrives, if my job ends, I'd take paid community care shifts before paying for more classes; the hands-on part buys some time before robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel my mind racing. I can start three plans in a day, yet none of them puts three months of rent in the bank by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why community care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I spent weekends helping my neighbour after a fall, and I liked being useful in a room rather than another chat window. I'd need to ask about lifting training and the actual hours, because a nice idea doesn't pay the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the centre offers you a temporary AI checking contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the contract if it paid enough and left time for care training, but I would ask its end date in writing. A two-month contract with no notice is not a bridge, even if the title sounds modern.

S2.quote: A two-month contract with no notice is not a bridge, even if the title sounds modern.
say: I would demand **paid routes** into other work and written notice before cuts.
I would reject the promise that every agent can become an **AI supervisor**.
think: I could lose both my **chat work** and the testing role to AGI by 2028.
I see the **2031 robot delay** buying hands-on care a little time, while my savings remain thin.
do: Meet the **staff group** now about notice and training pay.
Ask the **college** about a short health aide course and its costs.
Take **paid care shifts** if the centre job ends before paying for more classes.
feel: **Racing thoughts** and fear that plans cannot build savings fast enough.
fieldNote: She tests possible bridges against **pay and end dates**, not appealing job titles.
Her interest in care comes from helping a **neighbour**, but she checks training and hours first.

steps.text: Ask the staff group for written notice and training pay
Apply for paid community care shifts if chats end

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to negotiate a real learning budget if our centre stops treating training as a link in an email. I'd still test each new system hard, because mistakes do not become safe just because a machine writes them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can use the time to get a care certificate and actual experience before 2031. Yet care robots might arrive around 2034, so I would not borrow heavily for training without seeing what employers still need people to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a course fund this year and take one introductory care class while keeping my lead shifts. If the centre offers paid quality testing, I'd try it; in the first year after AGI arrives, if chat jobs disappear, I'd seek care shifts and ask employers what duties remain human before paying for another certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but I can work with a calendar like that. The trap would be using five years to collect certificates without ever trying the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask a care employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about physical help, medication routines, and time spent just talking with a client. If the answer is only paperwork, AGI will reach that job too, even before the care robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you stop the testing role from swallowing the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put one class on the calendar before accepting extra testing shifts. Jo, my colleague, would tell me if I was taking every late shift and pretending I could study later.

S3.quote: The trap would be using five years to collect certificates without ever trying the work.
say: I would seek a **learning budget** and keep testing AI errors.
I would warn that a machine-written answer still needs **checking** when money or care is involved.
think: I could gain **care experience** before 2031, unlike in the two-year picture.
I see **2034 robots** making a costly stack of certificates a poor bet.
do: Start a **course fund** and take one introductory care class this year.
Try a paid **quality testing** shift if offered.
Seek **care shifts** after AGI if chat jobs end, checking which duties need people.
feel: **Anxious**, with enough time to test the next job in person.
fieldNote: Daria thinks of learning as an **experiment**, not a promise that a certificate guarantees work.
She distinguishes 2031 thinking AI from **2034 care robots** and checks the actual duties between them.

steps.text: Start a course fund and take an introductory care class
Transfer part of each lead shift pay into the course fund
Apply for community care shifts if chat jobs end
Try a paid quality testing shift if offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our team to make the centre pay for useful training during the decade, and to keep telling customers when a person is checking a hard case. Ten years is long enough to change the job more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may be well into a different field by 2036, which makes this less like a deadline on my current badge. Still, AGI takes the thinking parts first, and robots around 2039 could reshape care work too; I should build skills that matter in a room with a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the lead role, save each payday and take one care class before signing up for a full course. Over the decade I'd ask for paid trial shifts to see if I can stand the work; in the first year after 2036, I'd leave the centre only if its hours vanish or the care role has a clear, paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious and watchful. The extra years make a trial possible instead of a leap into the dark.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay at the centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the centre gave us time to check difficult cases and paid leads properly, I could stay for quite a while. I won't stay for a shiny title that hides fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep mentioning paid trials. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A weekend with my neighbour wasn't the same as a full week in care. I want to see the lifting, the travel, and the pay before I plan my life around it.

S4.quote: A weekend with my neighbour wasn't the same as a full week in care.
say: I would ask the centre to fund **useful training** over the decade.
I would keep customers informed when a **person checks** a difficult case.
think: By 2036 I may already work elsewhere, but **thinking tasks** still change first.
I need to test face-to-face duties because care robots may arrive around **2039**.
do: Keep **lead shifts** while saving each payday.
Take one **care class** and ask for paid trial shifts before a full course.
Leave the centre after 2036 only for lost hours or a **clear care opening**.
feel: **Curious and watchful**, with time to try work before committing.
fieldNote: A decade lets Daria **sample care work** instead of guessing from one weekend helping a neighbour.
She would stay at the centre for **fair pay** and time to check difficult cases.

steps.text: Keep leading chat shifts while the centre pays full hours
Save a fixed amount from each payday for training
Take one care class and request paid trial shifts
Apply for a paid care opening if centre hours disappear

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest. I could lose chat work and the testing job before I can pay for retraining, so written notice and paid time for a real course would matter. I'd also want an honest job trial, with the hours and wages on paper.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who has to explain a wrong answer to the customer. I'd happily test the tool, but the centre has to give a named worker time to put a bad refund right instead of making the customer start again.

headlineQuote: I'd happily test the tool, but the centre has to give a named worker time to put a bad refund right instead of making the customer start again.
portrait: Daria, **27**, leads late contact centre chats and uses AI daily, drawing on a two-year college diploma and strong account checking.
Her **low pay**, savings below one month of expenses, and few nearby contact centre jobs make even normal bills stressful.
She quickly proposes **tool trials** and paid quality testing, while recognising that one new role may replace several agents.
Fast **2028 AGI** worries her most; a longer runway lets her test paid care work and avoid expensive training guesses.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove both chat work and the testing role before she can pay for a new course.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid course time, and an honest job trial with wages and hours on paper would help her move.
